findings.title: No test for non-integer results or rounding
findings.explanation: All the new cases use 3000 over 30 days, so every expected value is a whole number (3000, 0, 2000). The PR is meant to cover edge cases, but it skips the most likely proration bug: amounts that don't divide evenly, such as 1000 cents after 10 of 30 days, which gives 666.67. Add a case with an uneven amount or period and assert the intended rounding (floor, round or ceil, in integer cents). Also check that the 2000 expectation holds exactly and isn't affected by floating-point error from something like `amount * (remaining / total)`.

findings.title: Degenerate and invalid periods are not covered
findings.explanation: The PR description lists the edge cases covered, but there is no test for a zero-length period (start equals end), which could divide by zero and return NaN, or for an inverted period (end before start). A zero amount and sub-day cancellation times (for example mid-day) are also missing. Add tests that pin down the expected behavior, either a defined value or a thrown error.

findings.title: Repeated start/end setup in every test
findings.explanation: Every test redeclares the same `start` and `end` dates. Hoist them to shared constants in the `describe` block, or use `beforeEach`, to cut duplication and make the tests easier to read.

findings.title: Test name is tied to specific numbers and the PR calls it a 'partial month'
findings.explanation: The name 'refunds two thirds after ten days of a thirty-day period' only describes this one data set. April is a full 30-day month, so the test shows a partial elapsed period, not a partial month. Consider a more general name such as 'refunds the unused fraction of the period', and add a comment or a case with a different month length (31 or 28 days) to show that the day count comes from the dates.
